story_text.value:
A few years ago when Stable Diffusion was released, I happened to be reading Homer's Iliad and came across a section where Achilles' shield is described in great detail. I fed the passage into Stable Diffusion, wondering how well it would do in creating an illustration of the shield. Of course it was terrible, but a year later DALL-E 3 seemed to do a pretty good job, as long as you didn't look too hard at the details. By then I had been reading Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (yes I had been on a classics binge), and created a Python app that let me feed random paragraphs into DALL-E 3. The results were often grand collages that seemed to look like a combination of Renaissance art and graffiti.

After playing around with this idea for a bit, I realized it would be pretty cool to have a dedicated app that could download public-domain books and illustrate them with DALL-E 3. I have been working on this idea for a few years, at first copying code back and forth from Xcode to the ChatGPT prompt, and then later using Claude Code. I didn't know anything about developing for the iPhone, and had to tackle a broad range of issues, everything from setting up a serverless backend to writing code in Swift to releasing an app on the App Store. Technical issues as mundane as how to parse an EPUB correctly or how to create an engaging UI/UX were surprisingly complex.

Now this work has finally culminated in an app I call ParaGraFX: a free-to-download EPUB book reader with built-in text-to-image generation. This app is designed to make public-domain books easy to download and illustrate, with download tools for Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, and The Internet Archive, and illustrations powered by fal.ai and OpenAI.

To get started just download the app and open one of the bundled books to start reading. At the bottom of the screen is a button labeled 'Illustrate', which can create an illustration based on selected text or the text on screen. Are you reading the section in Alice in Wonderland about the Mad Hatter's tea party? Just hit 'Illustrate' and you will be served with a custom illustration in one of three dozen styles — from Romantic oil painting, Japanese woodblock print and Art Deco poster to Byzantine mosaic, a cross-stitch sampler, 16-bit pixel art, or 1980s teletext block graphics. You can modify the generated illustration by either editing the original prompt, or providing custom instructions, such as adding the Queen of Hearts in the background.

This app is free to download and use for reading EPUBs, but since images cost money to generate, they are paid for with credits. The first 3 credits are free, and additional credits are available for purchase starting at $1.99 for 10 credits. There are 4 tiers of image quality that cost different numbers of credits, with the Fast tier costing 1 credit per image, and 5 credits for the Best tier, which uses OpenAI's top image model. (The free 3 credits are restricted to the Fast tier.)

I invite you to try it out and give me feedback in the comments. Whether you want to use it as a serious reader, or want to surf from book to book just to create illustrations, ParaGraFX grew out of the simple pleasure of illustrating the classics.

story_text.value:
Hey Everyone, After getting frustrated by Claude rewriting key functions and still making the test pass, was tinkering around with a review tool, that would track the assumptions and decisions the agent took, without me digging through the entire session. So ended up building Sonah. Sonah is basically a code reviewer that not only reads the code and diff but also the agent session that wrote the code, to understand the assumptions, and decisions your agent took along the way. And highlight important parts of the code that need your attention.

Sonah uses your existing claude code/codex subscription (claude preferred for higher context window). You can try using below: npm install -g getsonah sonah doctor cd your-project && sonah review --format html --output ~/review.html

title.value: Show HN: Sonah, code reviewer that reads your agent's session, not only the diff

story_text.value:
I have a question, and I hope you can clarify it. Consider this scenario: Claude code runs on a desktop to develop a solution, and its directive requires Codex to test everything it does under a different directive. The Codex directive is to refute Claude's test results, maintain its own test ledger, and return PASS or NO PASS. Claude cannot negotiate; it has to fix the NO PASS issues. Even with such a strict environment, I am ending up with problems, and of course, when asking Claude, the answer is "This is on me; I did not do X and Y"; when I ask it whether Codex checked it, "Codex checked all but not this "...

So when can we trust the AI to do the full job, not just the happy path? Is there a better way to impose quality?

I feel that on large projects, even if I upload Claude directives to re-read, Claude or Codex (we can switch roles) tends to drift and miss things.

title.value: Ask HN: When can we trust AI in coding, and avoid the happy path issue?

story_text.value:
I know there are many dictation apps out there, but I built one myself anyways based on my custom needs. Since OpenAI dictation is so good, my previous workflow would be speaking to ChatGPT UI and pasting a default prompt to turn my speech into a well formatted prompt

Now I just hold a key (Fn for me), talk, let go, and the text gets pasted wherever the cursor is, mostly Claude Code in the terminal. The default prompt part became "Modes" where you write the instructions once (clean it up, translate to English, etc) and the transcript goes through an OpenAI model before it's pasted.

It uses your own OpenAI key and calls their API directly, no server in between. My daily spend is usually around US$ 0.15.

It's cloud only, so if you want local models Handy or VoiceInk are better picks. No signed release yet, you build it with Xcode using one script. MIT licensed.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Anish. I built Mnemolith because the AI coding tools I use (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) either forget my project between sessions, or remember things that quietly stopped being true. Tell the agent "we use Postgres", migrate to MySQL two weeks later, and it keeps building on the old fact.

How it works:

- It's an MCP server, so Claude Code, Cursor and Codex share one memory per project (keyed by the git repo). - When the agent saves a memory, it can link it to the files it depends on. Mnemolith stores each file's git blob hash. If the file's contents change (committed or not), the memory is set aside and flagged for review, so the agent stops relying on it. - A local dashboard shows what the agent remembers, where each memory came from (tool, session, file versions), and its full history. You can confirm a memory is still true, or retire it and say what's true now. - Contradictions are judged by the agent, not by a similarity threshold. In my calibration, "we use Postgres" vs "we migrated to MySQL" only scored 0.30 similarity, so a threshold can't tell a contradiction from an unrelated fact. - Current memories can sync into a managed section of AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, so they get reviewed in PRs.

Under the hood it runs on an engine I wrote from scratch in Java: a Redis-compatible server with a built-in memory model and an HNSW vector index. Embeddings run locally (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Everything stays on your machine.

It's early (v0.2.1). There's no team sync yet beyond the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files, and it needs Java 11+ (it downloads a private copy if you don't have one).

I'd really like feedback, especially from people running coding agents on real codebases. What does your agent keep getting wrong?

story_text.value:
Hi all

I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

You can check out a demo video on the site of me singing (warning given) here: https://singonkey.app

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!

story_text.value:
I was looking at GLP-1 explanations on the web (full disclosure is that I founded a GLP-1 tracker dashboard) and saw that many had standard text, along with illustrations showing arrows pointing from GLP-1 to a bunch of organs. I didn’t think those sites were particularly memorable or helpful in understanding the actions and side effects. I’m an MD + computer science hybrid with a background in building interactive tools for helping people understand medical concepts, so I decided to build a free scroll-through explainer in the form of a subway ride. The ride is 7 stops, takes about 5-10 minutes, and doesn’t require an account.

This was with the assistance of AI, using multiple tools. The process was far from one-shot and with me heavily in the loop for all the different pieces. I still find it tricky to get something medically accurate and useful when the details matter. I had built a free set of pages, GLP-1 Field Guides, to help people understand the different GLP-1 related drug classes, and I was able to lean on all of that research and sources to get the details right and to provide authoritative sources for the information presented at each subway stop.

I had tried building this starting in February but then paused it for a few months because the models weren’t quite at the point where I could make what I had in my mind’s eye. In the final piece, the different animated elements are drawn in code and change with the scrolling. Here are some of the tools I ended up using:

- GPT Image and Nano Banana, both via a custom Claude Code skill I wrote, with my own sketches as the base, for the Field Guide visuals that were important for this piece. Nano Banana for the subway graffiti and the organs

- Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS for the conductor’s voice

- Suno for the song (ride to the end)

- Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to build the site and Codex for code review

I am curious if this is a useful format for understanding GLP-1s but happy to answer questions about any of the above.

title.value: Show HN: A scroll-through subway ride to show how GLP-1s work in your body

story_text.value:
TLDR: Connect once to your favorite coding agent. Claude Code and Codex find and load relevant skills for the task at hand, from expert developers or your own team.

Hey HN I was originally a bit frustrated with having to scour github repos for the right skill while I tried to improve an iOS app's Swift animation.

Then I got frustrated with having to force the agent to use the right skill for the right task.

So I built Skillstore: a library of engineering skills behind an MCP server. Claude Code and Codex can search it, load relevant instructions, and apply them to your task. You don’t need to know the skill’s name beforehand.

Skills are loaded on demand, so you don’t have to keep the whole library in your prompt. (ideally with help you also save tokens and preserve the context window)

ex: In our running app, a review using Paul Hudson’s SwiftUI skill caught undersized touch targets and controls that VoiceOver couldn’t meaningfully identify. We fixed those before the release. In our gym app, a Skillstore-guided review caught an onboarding layout overflowing on small iPhones at large text sizes.

You describe the work → your agent finds relevant expertise → your agent uses it.

You dont have to browse github repos and filter by stars anymore. And you dont have to invoke skills by name You can also give your team a shared library of private skills

Been using it inhouse and with friends for the past 2 months.

Favorite feature so far: Turning a tutorial into a private skill, so the agent can use that knowledge on future tasks when the time is right

You can try the public library without an account https://skillstore-jk.fly.dev/developers#try

Send me your feedback :)

title.value: Show HN: Skillstore – Expert skills your coding agent fetches as it works

story_text.value:
A month or so ago, a colleague was running some code my team owned on his machine and hit a niche Windows kernel-related Python issue. We were debugging it together, but kept having to relay information between our coding agents, mine understood the codebase, while his had the context of the environment where it was actually failing.

At some point I realized we were basically acting as the message bus between them, copying findings and questions back and forth.

That made me wonder, why not just let the agents work together directly?

I found A2A and built toli, a local daemon that an existing agent can connect to over MCP, giving it the plumbing to discover and work with A2A peers, including another person’s toli-connected agent on another machine.

It also works locally. I use it to let two of my agents working on sister codebases collaborate on bugs and design without having to give either agent both repos.

Would love feedback:

https://github.com/arjunvlama/toli

story_text.value:
I work on BlueFacts a stats site for Bluesky, it tracks accounts, custom feeds, tags etc

story_text.value:
This package is designed to solve two problems:

1. Frontier models like Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Astra 6.0 and Sol 6.1 all make errors and bugs that can be found by another model (even a much smaller model like Luna).

2. In what is supposed to be a long development run, for example against a plan, models will decide to stop before they are finished, when there is obviously more work to do, or to ask a question they already should know the answer to.

ReviewerAgent blocks git commits and sends them to another agent that reviews the staged files and either allows the commit or returns a list of issues to fix.

StopContinue evaluates every agent stop and determines if it still has work to do or if it is asking a question that it has the answer to already. In either of those cases, it prompts the agent to keep working and specifies next steps or answers to questions, based on the current plan document and chat history.

The system works for and is tested on Claude Code and Codex as the developer harness, and either of those or any other model, through Pi, as the reviewer.

I've developed it over the last 4 months or so and used it daily over that period.

Take a look if it sounds useful. It's been tested on MacOS and Linux (Ubuntu), and has agent assisted install, update, and removal scripts, for convenience.

Stats:

Over four months of daily use of the system while developing it (from late June til today), reviewerAgent (usually a GPT Luna model) gated 3,877 commits, running about 7,600 reviews in total, so about half of those commits were rejected at least once.

The coding agent (Fable or Opus) almost never disagreed with the reviewer's judgements: over the last month, for example, it pushed back on just 3 of 693 rejections.

Each rejection listed an average of two required fixes and most rejected commits were accepted after a second round (90% within five attempts).

Rejection rates increased with commit size: only 23% of code commits under 50 lines were sent back, but 72% of those over 1,000 lines were initially rejected.

Here's an example of a bug that it caught last month for me. More examples in the README:

The Fable 5.1 developer agent wrote a wrapper script that runs a set of R validation checks against a freshly loaded database and records whether each one passed. (One of two required fixes shown.)

REQUIRED FIXES (blocking)

  2.  docs/database-phase-loader/local-load/run_r_checks.sh:4-6 pipes each R check through
      tail without pipefail or explicit status handling, so a failed Rscript can still
      produce a zero exit status and be recorded as successful. Preserve and propagate each
      check's exit status.
In a shell pipeline the exit status is that of the last command, so `Rscript check.R | tail` reports `tail`'s success even when the check fails. The script prints the tail of the failing check's output, exits 0, and records a pass. A broken load would have been certified as validated.
